title: A differential equation: a rule that gives the rate from the state

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives. The ones in this book are first-order: each gives the rate of change of a quantity at a moment as a rule in its state, in the time, or in both. For body weight W in kilograms and time t in days, the form is dW/dt = f(W, t).

Such an equation has many solutions. An initial value, the state at one stated time, picks out one of them. The equation and the initial value together are an initial-value problem, and a function solves it only if it satisfies both.

With expenditure a straight line in weight, rising by epsilon, written ε, kilocalories a day for each kilogram, and a step change ΔEI in intake from a steady starting weight W0, the equation is:

ρ × dW/dt = ΔEI − ε × (W − W0),    with W = W0 at t = 0

This is Equation 1 of Polidori and colleagues (2016) with its physical activity and urinary glucose terms set to zero, rearranged.

A forward step, which is Euler’s method taken one step at a time, approximates a solution. From the state at time t, compute the rate from the equation. Then take the state at t + h to be about W(t) + h × (the rate at t). Each step holds the rate fixed across one interval of length h, as one rectangle does in a running total.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Over a day, the change in the body’s stored energy is what came in minus what went out.

dES/dt = EI − EE

ES is the energy stored in the body, in kilocalories. EI is energy intake and EE is energy expenditure, both in kilocalories a day.

Say each kilogram of weight gained or lost carries a fixed amount of energy. Call it rho, written ρ, in kilocalories per kilogram.

ρ × dW/dt = EI − EE

That line is true whenever ρ is fixed. The line above it is always true. Neither predicts anything. A smaller body spends less, so EE depends on the weight itself.

So write EE as a rule in W. It says each kilogram of weight adds a fixed number of kilocalories a day to expenditure. Call that number epsilon, written ε.

EE = EE0 + ε × (W − W0)
EI = EI0 + ΔEI
EI0 = EE0, because the weight was steady at the start
so ρ × dW/dt = EI − EE = ΔEI − ε × (W − W0)

EE0 and EI0 are expenditure and intake at the start, when the weight was W0. ΔEI is the change in intake.

That is what a differential equation is: a rule that gives the rate from the state.

  • An answer to it is not a number. It is a whole curve of weight against time. You check a curve by putting it into the equation. The two sides have to agree at every moment, not only at the start.
  • Many curves obey the same rule. The starting weight picks out the one that is yours.

You can also walk the curve without a formula. Work out today’s rate from today’s weight. Move one day at that rate. Work out the new rate from the new weight. Move again.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Go back to Hall and colleagues’ man from Book 1. He weighs 100 kilograms and cuts his energy intake by 2 megajoules a day. The paper converts that for you: “2 MJ per day (480 kcal per day)”. So ΔEI, the change in intake, is minus 480 kilocalories a day.

Use 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram, the static rule’s own figure from Book 1.

For ε, Hall and Guo (2017) give expenditure rising with weight “with a slope of about 20–30 kcal/d per kg”. Take the lower end, 20 kilocalories a day for each kilogram. The man’s equation is then:

7716.18 × dW/dt = −480 − 20 × (W − 100),    with W = 100 at t = 0

On the right, the cut in intake, plus the fall in expenditure since the start. When W is below 100, W − 100 is negative. So minus 20 times it is positive, and it eats into the deficit.

Start with the curve that fails. The static rule says his weight falls in a straight line.

480 divided by 7716.18 = 0.06221
W(t) = 100 − 0.06221 × t

Put that line into the equation a year in, at t = 365. The line’s slope is −0.06221 kilograms a day on every day, so the left side is this.

7716.18 times 0.06221 = 480.02

About minus 480. Now the right side needs the weight at day 365.

0.06221 times 365 = 22.71
100 minus 22.71 = 77.29

His weight on the line is 77.29 kilograms, 22.71 below the start.

20 times 22.71 = 454.2
480 minus 454.2 = 25.8

The right side is about minus 25.8. The left side is minus 480. The two sides disagree by more than 450 kilocalories a day. The straight line starts at the right weight and is not a solution. It solves the equation only when ε is 0, that is, when expenditure ignores weight.

Now the curve that works.

W(t) = 100 − 24 × (1 − e(-t/385.809))

Each is a ratio of the equation’s own numbers.

480 divided by 20 = 24
7716.18 divided by 20 = 385.809

This is section 4’s W = L plus (W0 minus L) e(-kt), with L = 76, W0 − L = 24 and k = 1 divided by 385.809.

Check it the way any candidate is checked: the start, then both sides. At t = 0, e(0) is 1. So 1 − 1 is 0, and W is 100. The initial value holds.

For the rate, use section 4’s rule: the derivative of e(-kt) is −k × e(-kt). The derivative of W is then this.

dW/dt = −24 × (1 divided by 385.809) × e(-t/385.809)
24 divided by 385.809 = 0.06221

In symbols the check is two lines. The left side uses the rule for e(-kt); the right side is algebra.

left: 7716.18 × dW/dt = −480 × e(-t/385.809)
right: −480 − 20 × (−24) × (1 − e(-t/385.809)) = −480 + 480 − 480 × e(-t/385.809)

Both come to minus 480 times e(-t/385.809). The deficit starts at 480 kilocalories a day and shrinks towards nothing as the weight falls.

Now walk it without the formula, one day at a time. On day 0 the weight is 100, so the bracket is 0 and the rate is the static rule’s.

480 divided by 7716.18 = 0.062207
100 minus 0.062207 = 99.937793

On day 1 the weight is 99.937793, which is 0.062207 below the start.

20 times 0.062207 = 1.24414
480 minus 1.24414 = 478.75586
478.75586 divided by 7716.18 = 0.062046
99.937793 minus 0.062046 = 99.875747

About 99.8757 on day 2. The formula gives 99.8759. The steps drift a little from the curve, because each one holds the rate fixed for a whole day while the true rate keeps falling. A smaller step drifts less.

So a different step gives a different answer. By day 90, one-day steps give 95.00 and thirty-day steps 94.83; the formula gives 95.01. A model run is also a choice of step. The next rung shows when too large a step makes the answer run away.

Run the formula for three years and put the static line beside it. A second curve uses the top of Hall and Guo’s range, ε = 30.

day    static rule, ε = 0 ε = 20 kcal/day per kg ε = 30 kcal/day per kg
0    100    100    100
90    94.40    95.01    95.28
180    88.80    91.05    91.95
365    77.29    85.32    87.87
545    66.10    81.84    85.92
730    54.59    79.62    84.94
1095 31.88    77.40    84.23

All three columns come from one equation. Only ε differs. With ε at 0, the loss never slows. With any ε above 0, the loss slows and flattens.

The same equation can also be run backwards. Polidori and colleagues (2016) had weights and no reliable intake. They put the weight and its rate into their Equation 1 and read off ΔEI. The intake change they report is an output of the equation, not a measurement.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The value of ρ here is the static rule’s 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram, borrowed as a stand-in. For a real body, ρ “need not be a constant”, as Chow and Hall (2008) put it. It changes with what the weight lost is made of. So the curves in the table have the right shape and not Hall’s timing.

The straight line for expenditure is an approximation. It is safest for changes small enough that one slope describes them.

points.html: The energy balance identity predicts nothing on its own. A prediction appears only when someone writes expenditure, and perhaps intake, as a rule in weight. When you read a projection built “on energy balance”, find that rule.
A curve that starts at the right weight is not thereby a solution. Check a claimed solution at the start and at a later time, on both sides of the equation.
“Cut 480 kilocalories and you run a 480 deficit every day” is the static rule. Correct a trainee who carries the day-one deficit forward: the cut stays the same; the deficit does not.
When you step an equation forward, work the rate out again from the new state at every step.
Keep the units in step: ρ in kilocalories per kilogram and intake in kilocalories a day give kilograms a day.
Use it for the shape of a response and for modest changes. For one person’s timetable over years, use a validated model, and say in writing which one you used.
When a paper reports intake “calculated” from repeated weighings, read it as the output of an equation. It moves with the ρ and the ε put in.

blocks.prompt:
Polidori and colleagues (2016) calculate a change in energy intake from repeated weighings with their Equation 1. The paper writes BW for body weight. A letter or digit after a symbol is a label: i marks the interval, and 0 the start.

ΔEIi = ρ × (dBWi/dt) + ε × (BWi − BW0) + (Δδ divided by (1 − β)) × BW0 + UGE

For each symbol, say what it stands for and its unit, as far as the paper tells you. Then say which two terms this section set to zero, and what setting each to zero assumes.
blocks.answer:
Take the symbols from left to right.

  • ΔEIi: the change in energy intake from the start, in the interval i. Kilocalories a day.
  • ρ: rho, “the effective energy density associated with the body weight change”. Kilocalories per kilogram.
  • dBWi/dt: the rate of change of body weight over the interval, worked out from the moving average of the weighings. Kilograms a day.
  • ε: epsilon, which “defined how energy expenditure depends on body weight”. Kilocalories a day for each kilogram.
  • BWi − BW0: the weight in the interval minus the weight at the start. Kilograms.
  • Δδ: the change in physical activity. The paper says it is “often assumed to be zero” when there are no measurements of activity.
  • β: beta, which “accounts for the adaptation of energy expenditure during a diet perturbation”. Table 1 gives it as 0.24, with no unit.
  • UGE: urinary glucose excretion, “the energy losses as a result of increased urinary excretion of glucose with canagliflozin treatment”. Table 1 gives it in kcal/d, so kilocalories a day.

Check the units of the first two terms on the right. Kilocalories per kilogram times kilograms a day is kilocalories a day. Kilocalories a day per kilogram times kilograms is kilocalories a day. Both match the left side.

This section set the activity term and the glucose term to zero. Setting Δδ to zero assumes physical activity did not change. Setting UGE to zero assumes no extra glucose is lost in the urine, as for a person not taking a drug that raises it. What remains, rearranged, is ρ × dW/dt = ΔEI − ε × (W − W0).

blocks.prompt: A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. They ask: “If energy in minus energy out is always true, why does the same diet give smaller losses each month?” Explain, with the equation, and expect them to want the mechanism.
blocks.answer:
Start from what they already accept. Write the identity in rate form.

ρ × dW/dt = EI − EE

It is true whenever ρ is fixed, and it cannot predict tomorrow. Tomorrow’s EE is not known today.

Then add the one piece of physiology. A smaller body spends less. Draw expenditure as a straight line rising with weight, slope ε. Rewrite the right side as the cut in intake minus ε times the change in weight.

ρ × dW/dt = ΔEI − ε × (W − W0)

Now point at the second term. On day one it is zero, so the whole cut is the deficit. As W falls below W0, the term takes a bite out of the deficit. The same cut buys a smaller deficit, so a slower loss.

Put numbers in if they want them. Hall’s 100 kg man cuts 480 kilocalories a day. With ε at 20, once he is 10 kilograms down the fall in expenditure is 200 kilocalories a day. His deficit is then 280, not 480.

Close with what the equation does not say. It does not say ε is 20 for this patient. It does not include appetite rising as weight falls. And it is a straight-line simplification.

blocks.prompt: A rule gives the rate of change of y as dy/dt = 6 − 0.5 × y. Work out the rate when y is 4, when y is 12, and when y is 20.
blocks.answer:
Put each value of y into the right side.

0.5 times 4 = 2
6 minus 2 = 4
0.5 times 12 = 6
6 minus 6 = 0
0.5 times 20 = 10
6 minus 10 = -4

The rates are 4, 0 and minus 4. The rate depends on where y is. Below 12, y rises. Above 12, y falls.

blocks.prompt:
Say which of these are differential equations. For each one that is, say whether the rate depends on the state y, or on the time t alone.

  1. y = 3t + 2
  2. dy/dt = 3t + 2
  3. dy/dt = −0.2 × y
  4. E = 4P + 9F + 4C
blocks.answer:
A differential equation holds an unknown function and its derivative.

  1. is not one. It gives y directly and holds no derivative.

  2. is one. Its rate depends on t alone. An antiderivative of the right side solves it, which is the earlier section’s move.

  3. is one. Its rate depends on the state y. You cannot integrate the right side without already knowing y at every time, which is what you are looking for.

  4. is not one. It is a weighted sum of three quantities, with no rate in it.

Equations like (c) are the ones this section is about.

blocks.prompt: Take dy/dt = 6 − 0.5 × y with y = 4 at t = 0. Take three forward steps of size 1. Give y at t = 1, 2 and 3.
blocks.answer:
Each step: rate from the current y, then new y = old y + 1 × rate.

6 minus 0.5 times 4 = 4
4 plus 4 = 8
6 minus 0.5 times 8 = 2
8 plus 2 = 10
6 minus 0.5 times 10 = 1
10 plus 1 = 11

About 8 at t = 1, 10 at t = 2 and 11 at t = 3. Each step is smaller than the one before, because the rate falls as y rises.

blocks.prompt: Take the initial-value problem dy/dt = 6 − 0.5 × y, with y = 4 at t = 0. Check whether y = 12 − 8 × e(-0.5t) solves it. Then compare its value at t = 2 with the forward steps you would get from step size 1.
blocks.answer:
The start first. At t = 0, e(0) is 1.

12 minus 8 = 4

The initial value holds.

The left side. With k = 0.5, the derivative of e(-kt) is −k × e(-kt).

dy/dt = −8 × (−0.5) × e(-0.5t) = 4 × e(-0.5t)

The right side.

6 − 0.5 × (12 − 8 × e(-0.5t)) = 6 − 6 + 4 × e(-0.5t) = 4 × e(-0.5t)

The two sides match at every t, so the function solves the problem.

At t = 2 the exponent is minus 1, and e(-1) is 0.3679.

8 times 0.3679 = 2.9432
12 minus 2.9432 = 9.0568

About 9.06. Forward steps of size 1 give 10 at t = 2. The steps overshoot, because each holds the first rate of its step for the whole step while the true rate is falling.

blocks.prompt:
Three people offer a solution to dy/dt = 6 − 0.5 × y with y = 20 at t = 0.

  1. y = 12 + 8 × e(-0.5t)
  2. y = 20 − 4t
  3. y = 12 + 4 × e(-0.5t)

Which one solves the initial-value problem? Say what is wrong with each of the other two.
blocks.answer:
Check each at t = 0, then on both sides.

  1. At t = 0, 12 + 8 = 20. The start holds. The left side is −4 × e(-0.5t). The right side is 6 − 6 − 4 × e(-0.5t), the same. (a) solves it.

  2. At t = 0, y = 20. The start holds. The left side is minus 4 at every t. The right side is 6 − 0.5 × (20 − 4t), which is −4 + 2t. The two agree only at t = 0. At t = 1:

20 minus 4 = 16
0.5 times 16 = 8
6 minus 8 = -2

Minus 2 on the right against minus 4 on the left. (b) is not a solution.

  1. The left side is −2 × e(-0.5t). The right side is 6 − 6 − 2 × e(-0.5t), the same, so it obeys the rule. But at t = 0 it gives 12 + 4 = 16, not 20. It is a solution of the equation and the wrong member of the family.

blocks.prompt: Hall and Guo (2017) use a cut of 300 kilocalories a day from the diet. On the first day of the cut, the weight has not yet moved, so the whole cut is the deficit. With ρ = 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram, the static rule’s figure, work out dW/dt in kilograms a day and in kilograms a week.
blocks.answer:
On day one, W equals W0, so the ε term is zero. The equation is 7,716.18 × dW/dt = −300.

300 divided by 7716.18 = 0.03888
0.03888 times 7 = 0.27216

dW/dt is about minus 0.0389 kilograms a day, or minus 0.272 kilograms a week.

Check the unit. Kilocalories a day divided by kilocalories per kilogram leaves kilograms a day.

This rate holds on day one only. Every later day, the weight is lower and the rate is smaller.

blocks.prompt: Same cut of 300 kilocalories a day, same ρ = 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram. Hall and Guo put the slope of expenditure against weight at 20 to 30 kilocalories a day per kilogram. A person, made up for this problem, is now 4 kilograms below their starting weight. Work out dW/dt at each end of that range.
blocks.answer:
The equation is 7,716.18 × dW/dt = −300 − ε × (W − W0), with W − W0 = −4.

With ε = 20:

20 times 4 = 80
300 minus 80 = 220
220 divided by 7716.18 = 0.02851

With ε = 30:

30 times 4 = 120
300 minus 120 = 180
180 divided by 7716.18 = 0.02333

About minus 0.0285 and minus 0.0233 kilograms a day. On day one it was minus 0.0389. Four kilograms in, the loss has slowed by a quarter to two-fifths, depending on ε. The range of ε is carried into the answer. It is not a rounding error to be smoothed away.

blocks.prompt:
Polidori and colleagues computed dW/dt from weighings 52 days apart. A person, made up for this problem, weighed 98.0 kilograms at the start. They weighed 96.4 kilograms at one weighing and 95.8 kilograms at the next, 52 days later.

Use ρ = 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram and ε = 30 kilocalories a day per kilogram, Polidori’s round figure for the change in expenditure. Take W − W0 at the later weighing. Work out ΔEI with ρ × dW/dt = ΔEI − ε × (W − W0).
blocks.answer:
The rate first, from the two weighings.

95.8 minus 96.4 = -0.6
0.6 divided by 52 = 0.011538

dW/dt is about minus 0.011538 kilograms a day. Now the change since the start.

98.0 minus 95.8 = 2.2

W − W0 is minus 2.2 kilograms. Rearrange the equation for ΔEI by adding ε × (W − W0) to both sides.

ΔEI = ρ × dW/dt + ε × (W − W0)
7716.18 times 0.011538 = 89.03
30 times 2.2 = 66
89.03 plus 66 = 155.03

ΔEI is about minus 155 kilocalories a day. Both terms are negative here. The weight is still falling, and it is below the start.

blocks.prompt:
Polidori and colleagues describe a commercial weight-loss programme. “After 1 year, the average energy intake was practically at baseline levels while body weight was still reduced by ~5 kg.”

Take ΔEI = 0 and W − W0 = −5 kilograms (the ~ means about). Use ρ = 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram and ε at each end of Hall and Guo’s 20 to 30 kilocalories a day per kilogram. Work out dW/dt, and the change over the next 30 days if it held. Say which way the weight is heading.
blocks.answer:
The right side is 0 − ε × (−5), which is plus 5 × ε.

With ε = 20:

20 times 5 = 100
100 divided by 7716.18 = 0.012960
0.012960 times 30 = 0.3888

With ε = 30:

30 times 5 = 150
150 divided by 7716.18 = 0.019440
0.019440 times 30 = 0.5832

dW/dt is plus 0.013 to plus 0.019 kilograms a day. Over 30 days that is about 0.39 to 0.58 kilograms, if the rate held. It will not quite hold: as the weight rises the bracket shrinks and the rate falls. The weight is heading back up.

The paper describes this course as a plateau “followed by slow weight regain”. The equation gives the same direction, from intake alone and the lower expenditure of a smaller body. Nobody’s effort appears anywhere in it.

blocks.prompt: Hall and colleagues’ 100 kg man cuts intake by 480 kilocalories a day. Use ρ = 7,716.18 kilocalories per kilogram and ε = 20 kilocalories a day per kilogram. Take three forward steps of 30 days each, and give his weight at day 90. Then give the static rule’s weight at day 90, which is 100 − 480 × 90 / 7,716.18.
blocks.answer:
Step 1, from day 0. The bracket is zero.

480 divided by 7716.18 = 0.062207
0.062207 times 30 = 1.86621
100 minus 1.86621 = 98.13379

Step 2, from 98.13379. The weight is 1.86621 below the start.

20 times 1.86621 = 37.3242
480 minus 37.3242 = 442.6758
442.6758 divided by 7716.18 = 0.057370
0.057370 times 30 = 1.7211
98.13379 minus 1.7211 = 96.41269

Step 3, from 96.41269. The weight is 3.58731 below the start.

20 times 3.58731 = 71.7462
480 minus 71.7462 = 408.2538
408.2538 divided by 7716.18 = 0.052909
0.052909 times 30 = 1.58727
96.41269 minus 1.58727 = 94.82542

About 94.83 kilograms at day 90. The static rule:

480 times 90 = 43200
43200 divided by 7716.18 = 5.5986
100 minus 5.5986 = 94.4014

About 94.40 kilograms. The two differ by about 0.4 kilograms at 90 days, and the gap widens every month after. The curve formula from the illustration gives 95.01 at day 90. Thirty-day steps overshoot the loss a little, 94.83 against 95.01, because each holds its first rate for 30 days.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

the man’s equation is 7716.18 × dW/dt = −480 − 20 × (W − 100), starting at 100 kg
on day 0, W − 100 is 0, so dW/dt = −480 / 7716.18 = −0.062207 kg a day
over 90 days: 0.062207 × 90 = 5.5986 kg
so the equation predicts 100 − 5.5986 = 94.40 kg at day 90
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the third. It takes the rate from day 0 and uses it for all 90 days. The equation gives a new rate every day from that day’s weight. By day 30 the weight is lower, so the ε term is no longer zero, and the rate is smaller.

Stepping properly, as in the problem above with 30-day steps, gives about 94.83 kilograms. The curve formula gives 95.01.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Lines one and two are correct. The day-0 rate is right. The error is to treat a rate at an instant as a rate for the whole stretch. That turns the model back into the static rule, which is exactly what 94.40 is.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a person cuts intake by 300 kcal a day; ρ = 7716.18 kcal/kg; ε = 20
model: ρ × dW/dt = ΔEI + ε × (W − W0)
4 kg below the start: −300 + 20 × (−4) = −380
dW/dt = −380 / 7716.18 = −0.04925 kg a day
so at 4 kg down the loss has sped up from 0.0389 to 0.0492 kg a day
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the second: the sign in front of ε. The model should read ρ × dW/dt = ΔEI − ε × (W − W0).

Test it with the physiology. When W is below W0, the body is smaller, so expenditure is lower. Lower expenditure means less going out, so the deficit should shrink, not grow. With the minus sign:

20 times 4 = 80
300 minus 80 = 220
220 divided by 7716.18 = 0.02851

The rate is minus 0.0285 kilograms a day, slower than the day-one 0.0389, as it should be.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Every line after the second is correct arithmetic. A plus and a minus look alike in a methods section. The quick check is the direction: a model in which losing weight makes you lose faster runs away, and nobody’s weight does that.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

Hall’s man cuts intake by 2 MJ a day
ρ = 7716.18 kcal per kg
day one: dW/dt = −2 / 7716.18 = −0.000259 kg a day
over a year: 0.000259 × 365 = 0.0946 kg
so the cut barely moves his weight
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the third. It divides megajoules by kilocalories per kilogram. The units do not cancel to kilograms.

Convert the cut first. The paper gives it as 480 kilocalories a day.

480 divided by 7716.18 = 0.062207

Minus 0.0622 kilograms a day on day one, about 240 times the wrong figure.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Every line is correct arithmetic, and a small number after a division feels plausible. A unit check on line three catches it: megajoules a day divided by kilocalories per kilogram is not kilograms a day. So does a size check. A cut of 480 kilocalories a day moving weight by 95 grams in a year should stop anyone.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer to problem 8. The person weighed 98.0 kilograms at the start, then 96.4 and 95.8 kilograms at weighings 52 days apart. Take ρ = 7,716.18 and ε = 30. Find the step that broke.

dW/dt = (95.8 − 96.4) / 52 = −0.011538 kg a day
W − W0 = 95.8 − 96.4 = −0.6 kg
ΔEI = 7716.18 × (−0.011538) + 30 × (−0.6) = −89.03 − 18 = −107.03 kcal a day
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the second. W0 is the weight at the start of the study, 98.0 kilograms, not the weight at the previous weighing. The ε term is about how far expenditure has fallen since the start. That depends on the whole loss so far, not on the last 52 days.

98.0 minus 95.8 = 2.2
30 times 2.2 = 66
89.03 plus 66 = 155.03

ΔEI is about minus 155 kilocalories a day, not minus 107.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. The first line correctly uses the two latest weighings for the rate. Using the same two weighings for the change looks consistent. It mixes up two quantities: the rate is recent, and the change is since the start.

blocks.prompt:
A commentator writes: “Energy balance is only an accounting identity. Any weight prediction built on it is circular, because it just restates that calories in minus calories out equals the change in stores.” The commentator is made up for this problem.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: whether the prediction comes from the identity or from something added to it. Take Hall’s man, cutting 480 kilocalories a day, with ρ = 7,716.18. Work out his rate when he is 4 kilograms down, under three rules for expenditure.

ε = 0, expenditure ignores weight:

480 divided by 7716.18 = 0.06221

ε = 20:

20 times 4 = 80
480 minus 80 = 400
400 divided by 7716.18 = 0.05184

ε = 30:

30 times 4 = 120
480 minus 120 = 360
360 divided by 7716.18 = 0.04666

Three different rates, all obeying the same identity. So the commentator is half right. The identity alone predicts nothing. The prediction comes from the rule for expenditure that was added, and that rule is a claim about bodies, open to test. Nothing about it is circular.

What this does not establish. It does not show which ε is right, or that one straight line fits expenditure across a large loss. It does not show that ρ is constant; Chow and Hall say it need not be. And it says nothing about why intake or expenditure changed. Hall and Guo make that point about the identity itself.

blocks.prompt:
A review sentence reads: “Polidori and colleagues measured how much people’s eating changed, using weights taken 52 days apart.” The review is made up for this problem; the paper is real.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: whether the number depends on anything besides the weighings. Use the made-up person from problem 8: dW/dt = −0.011538 kilograms a day and W − W0 = −2.2 kilograms. Compute ΔEI = ρ × dW/dt + ε × (W − W0) three ways.

ρ = 7,716.18 and ε = 30, as before:

7716.18 times 0.011538 = 89.03
30 times 2.2 = 66
89.03 plus 66 = 155.03

ρ = 7,716.18 and ε = 20:

20 times 2.2 = 44
89.03 plus 44 = 133.03

ρ taken as the energy of body fat, 39.5 megajoules a kilogram (Book 1), which is 9,440.73 kilocalories, with ε = 30:

39500 divided by 4.184 = 9440.73
9440.73 times 0.011538 = 108.93
108.93 plus 66 = 174.93

The same two weighings give minus 133, minus 155 or minus 175 kilocalories a day. So the intake figure is calculated through a model, and it moves with the model’s constants. The paper’s own word is “calculated”.

What this does not establish. It does not show that Polidori’s figures are wrong. Their ρ and ε come from a model built on controlled feeding studies, not from these stand-ins. It does not tell you any one person’s intake; the paper “restricted our analysis to the group mean”. And it assumes activity did not change. The paper puts the bias from that at “<40 kcal/day when studying >100 individuals”. Say “calculated”, and name the model.
